The problem is cheating in online chess is impossible to enforce. And we don't want this burden to fall on FIDE, who should focus on making good tournaments instead.

Online has nothing to do with FIDE, and they certainly do not have the resources to enforce rules over casual online games. Thus they simply do not count whatever happens over there. It's up to the chess sites to enforce their own rules, and from what I see it is an impossible task to eliminate cheating online.

This is true for OTB too. FIDE does not care if there is a cheater at some local chess club. If a guy gets caught cheating while playing at a small club, he'll get kicked out of the club at most. Doesn't stop him from going pro if he wants to.

But if a player ever cheats in a FIDE tournament, they will come and hit him with the full force, because it is under their authority.

I know most people here play online and want their online games to be fair and clean, but really it's up to the chess sites to enforce this, and it is probably and impossible task I believe. So the best thing is to separate online and FIDE tournaments, as FIDE cannot be responsible for whatever nonsense happens online.

I really can't stand the idea of there being cheating in these top level tournaments.

I would like to believe in these top level people's play. When players say that a move is Fabi-like, or Magnus-like, or when on stream Hikaru says he wants to "pull a Naroditsky", it adds a human-like character to the game. It is frequently implied that even at the top level, players have particular and identifiable tendencies/flaws that other players learn and try to exploit. If a player cheats, it basically calls the entire perception of their "human player" and style into question.

The fact that at top OTB tournaments it's possible to cheat (not even too difficult, as stated by Naroditsky) means that at some level I have no choice but to trust the players, and trust the games. I didn't find that very difficult to do... until this whole Sinquefield situation. Even aside from the question of whether or not Hans cheated in the Magnus game, there is a ton of smoke- whether from the chess.com stuff, several of his OTB tournaments, the informed opinions of several GMs, interviews etc. If there is actually fire behind that smoke it could take years to sniff out, like it did for for that Rausis guy.

It all makes me wonder- how far precisely can a cheater go? Can a cheater, even when mired by suspicion, win the Candidates? Can they go on to be a reigning World Champion, cheating all the while for maybe only a few critical moments in important games?

I'm honestly a little soured on these top level tournaments now, and have less of a desire to follow them. Maybe I'll get over it, but in any case, I know at least for MY enjoyment, more stringent anti-cheating measures for top level games would be helpful.

I have attempted to verify the claims that Hans outperforms in broadcast tournaments. I have been unable to find any evidence for this claim. Note that I am not a statistician, so the below should be regarded critically.

Scope: Classical between 2020 and now, during which Hans progressed from 2465 to 2688 classical FIDE rating. Atlanta Kings checked games from 2019 to 2020, which seems pointless to me.

Sources: Games from scraping 365chess.com. Data on whether tournaments were broadcast by manually checking chess24, lichess, and chess.com events pages.

Null hypothesis: Hans does not overperform in tournaments depending on whether they are broadcast or not.

We define a overperformance metric as Hans' game score minus Hans' expected score given the elos of the two players, where the expected score is defined by FIDE as erfc(-eloDiff / ((2000.0/7) * sqrt(2))) / 2.

We run a standard two-sample t-test. It can be argued that samples are not independently distributed; for example, due to streaks and tilting. However, this effect should be minimal considering the number of games analyzed.

Number of broadcast games:  249
Number of non-broadcast games:  91
Broadcast overperformance mean:  0.07548174250316311
Non-broadcast overperformance mean:  0.043300909768091825
p:  0.45869142889543135
At alpha=0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis: there is no statistically significant evidence that Hans overperforms in either broadcast or nonbroadcast tournaments.

I have uploaded my Python code at https://pastebin.com/6EXSCH09 in case anyone wants to check my work or try this for other players. The most taxing part is to specify which tournaments are broadcast or not (e.g., some tournaments were broadcast on only one or two of lichess, chess.com, and chess24). If anyone knows of a data source that provides all games along with whether the tournament was broadcast live or not, please let me know.

If it makes sense I can make a top-level post later with a few graphs once people have checked that my math isn't totally off.

Finally, I'd like to note that none of this is really required. We already have several GMs stating that Hans is 2700 level for sure, plus his blitz/rapid ratings are commensurate with his classical rating. Still, there are other (doubtful) methods to cheat that would not be detected by the above naive analysis, so the claim here is only that there is no statistically significant difference between broadcast games and non-broadcast games.

Number of broadcast games:  249
Number of non-broadcast games:  91  
Broadcast overperformance mean:  0.006024096385542169  
Non-broadcast overperformance mean:  -0.13186813186813187  
p:  0.029076951080648467  
We reject the null hypothesis.
So at alpha=0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. There is some statistically significant difference in the expected win rate in games that were broadcast games as compared to those that were not broadcast.

In this dataset, he performs about as expected in the 249 games that where broadcast (overperformance ~= 0), but he does noticeable worse in the 91 games that where not broadcast (overperformance < 0).

Of course this does not mean anyone cheated, but it does highlight the fragility of using this statistical argument as strong evidence of innocence.
